title: Information-theoretic entropy imaging of quantum matter
authors: Chen Wu, Leonard W. Cao, Lingyuan Lyu, Liam Cohen, Jiahui Nie, Can Uzundal, Yujia Hu, Quanjin Wang, Ziying Yan, Sneh Pancholi, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Feng Wang, Andrea F. Young, Tarun Grover, Monica T. Allen
abstract: Phase transitions can generate intricate spatial organization invisible to spatially averaged probes, yet quantitative measures of this organization remain limited. Here we develop "entropy imaging," an information-theoretic technique that harnesses lossless compression to quantify spatial complexity, predictability, and order in quantum materials. Using this approach, emergent spatial textures can be imaged and converted into an experimentally-accessible observable: the computable information density (CID), a compression-based measure of information complexity that approaches the Shannon entropy rate in the large-system limit. Applied to millikelvin microwave impedance microscopy of graphene, the method reveals a pronounced maximum in the CID near quantum Hall transitions, a quantitative measure of the information-rich spatial organization of the critical landscape. A disordered Hofstadter model reproduces this behavior and shows that the CID can identify the quantum critical point from a sequence of images, without ensemble averaging over disorder realizations. The same framework tracks fractional quantum Hall transitions and resolves isolated fractional puddles that coexist with a disordered background. By contrast, the trivial band-edge crossover in a MoSe2/WS2 moiré heterobilayer exhibits qualitatively different behavior, suggesting that the pronounced CID enhancement observed at the quantum Hall critical point is not simply a generic feature of a conductive-insulating crossover. We further show that the geometric information encoded in CID is not reducible to a correlation length, and it can even distinguish spatial textures with identical multifractal statistics. Together, these results establish lossless compression as a framework for quantifying emergent spatial organization in quantum materials, with portability across imaging modalities and physical systems.
summary: This paper introduces 'entropy imaging,' an information-theoretic technique that uses lossless compression to quantify the spatial complexity of quantum materials. By calculating the Computable Information Density (CID), the authors demonstrate that this measure robustly identifies quantum critical points and tracks phase transitions across diverse experimental platforms, proving its utility beyond simple correlation length measurements.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of quantitatively measuring the intricate spatial organization and complexity within quantum materials, especially near phase transitions, which are often invisible to simple spatially averaged probes.
main_result: The developed 'entropy imaging' technique, using Computable Information Density (CID), successfully quantifies this spatial complexity, revealing pronounced maxima at quantum critical points in both experimental and simulated systems.
method: The core method is 'entropy imaging,' which employs lossless data compression (like LZ77) on spatial images to derive the CID, an information-theoretic measure related to the Shannon entropy rate.
model_or_system: The work is applied to diverse systems, including graphene near quantum Hall transitions, $	ext{MoSe}_2/	ext{WS}_2$ moiré heterobilayers, magnetic materials (FeRh, skyrmions), and disordered theoretical models like the Hofstadter model.
key_observables: Computable Information Density (CID), which quantifies spatial information complexity; Quantum Hall transition signatures; Correlation length ($\xi$).

main_assumptions: The CID is treated as a computable estimator of the spatial information complexity, and its relationship to thermodynamic entropy is asymptotic.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate CID peaks coinciding with quantum Hall transitions in graphene, and show CID tracking phase transitions (e.g., $	ext{1T-TaS}_2$ NC-IC transition) and structural changes across various imaging modalities.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the CID concept using quantum Hall transitions in graphene as the primary example, validates it against theoretical models (Hofstadter), and then demonstrates its broad applicability across multiple physical systems and imaging techniques (e.g., magnetic domain imaging, biofilm analysis).
why_interesting: The use of information theory (Kolmogorov complexity) to diagnose critical points and phase transitions provides a powerful, model-independent diagnostic tool for characterizing emergent order in complex quantum many-body systems.
